cues.text: Called with Two Words

A native of Bethsaida on the Sea of Galilee, the same town that gave the Church Peter and Andrew , Philip was among the earliest disciples called by Jesus, summoned with the same brief, direct invitation extended to Matthew : "follow me."

Philip's response, like theirs, was immediate — and it was immediately generous as well, for the very next thing Scripture records him doing is finding his friend Nathanael to share the news he could not keep to himself.
"We Have Found Him"

Philip's announcement to Nathanael carries the same unfiltered enthusiasm of a man who has just discovered something too large to hold alone: "we have found him of whom Moses in the Law and also the prophets wrote, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph."
When Nathanael responded with skepticism — "can anything good come out of Nazareth?"
— Philip did not argue theology or press an elaborate case; he simply said, "come and see," trusting the encounter itself to accomplish what argument alone could not.
A Practical Man Learning to Trust

Before the miraculous feeding of the five thousand, Jesus turned to Philip and asked, seemingly rhetorically, where they might buy enough bread to feed the assembled crowd — a question John's Gospel tells us was posed specifically to test him.
Philip's answer was entirely practical and entirely overwhelmed: two hundred denarii worth of bread, he calculated, would not be enough for each person to have even a little.

We recognize in this frank, arithmetic response a man not yet fully able to imagine what Christ's power could accomplish beyond ordinary calculation — and in Christ's patient willingness to work the miracle regardless, a Lord who forms his disciples' faith gradually, meeting their honest limitations rather than demanding an understanding they did not yet possess.
"Show Us the Father"

At the Last Supper, as Jesus spoke at length of his unity with the Father, it was Philip who gave voice to what may have been every disciple's deepest and most unspoken longing: "Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us."
Jesus's answer carries a note of gentle, searching surprise — "have I been with you so long, and yet you do not know me, Philip?
Whoever has seen me has seen the Father" — one of the clearest statements in the whole Gospel of Christ's own perfect unity with God the Father, drawn out by one Apostle's simple, honest request.
A Bridge to the Greeks

In the days before his Passion, Jesus was approached by a group of Greek pilgrims in Jerusalem who wished to see him — and they came first to Philip, perhaps because of his Greek name, asking him to serve as their intermediary.

Philip, in turn, brought the request to Andrew, and the two together carried it to Jesus, a small scene that has often been read as an early sign of the Gospel's coming spread beyond the Jewish people to the wider Gentile world.
A Martyrdom in Asia Minor

After Pentecost, tradition sends Philip to preach across Phrygia in Asia Minor, arriving eventually at Hierapolis , where his preaching won many converts but provoked the hostility of local authorities under the Emperor Domitian.

There, tradition holds, he was crucified — some accounts add, in a detail echoing several other Apostles, that he asked to be hung head downward, unwilling to be crucified in the same manner as his Lord.

Archaeologists have excavated a tomb structure amid the ruins of ancient Hierapolis, near the modern Turkish city of Denizli, long associated with Philip by local tradition — though its identification as his actual burial place remains a matter of tradition rather than settled proof.
Legacy

Philip's Gospel appearances — a man who shared good news immediately upon finding it, who calculated candidly even when overwhelmed, and who asked, on behalf of every believer since, to see the Father plainly — reveal an Apostle of genuine, unpretentious faith still growing in trust across the whole of his discipleship.
His feast, kept alongside St.

James the Less, remains a fitting pairing of two Apostles whose quiet, practical fidelity did as much to build the early Church as any more dramatic ministry, and whose simplest recorded words — come and see — remain, twenty centuries later, still the surest invitation the Gospel has ever offered.
